name: Add Values to an Empty List (Case 2)
description: Construct a program that creates a list of eight string values received from the user.
code:
#Step 1: Create an empty list
lst = []
#Step 2: Add the user inputs to the list one by one
for i in range(8):
    lst.append( input("Enter a value:") ) 
#Step 3: Print the list
print(lst)

commentList: You create an empty list named lst that will hold the eight string values the program reads from the user; this line sets up the container you will fill in the loop.
You use the assignment operator (=) to bind the name lst to an empty list literal ([]). The [] syntax makes a new empty list object so you can later call lst.append(...) to add items.

You must initialize the list before the for loop; if you omit this line and try to append to lst, you'll get a NameError because lst doesn't exist. Also note that () would make a tuple (which doesn't support append) and {} would make a dict or set, so use [] for a list.

Avoid naming your variable list because that would shadow Python's built-in list type and can cause confusion or bugs. Use a clear name like lst or values (a plural name helps show it's a collection).

As a best practice, prefer the literal [] for an empty list in simple code because it's concise and clear. Remember that the list can be changed after you create it, so appending inside the loop is the right way to collect user inputs.

commentList: You use this for-loop to repeat the next indented line eight times so the program asks for and adds eight values to the list.

In syntax terms: 'for' starts the loop, 'i' is the loop variable that changes each time, 'range(8)' produces the sequence 0,1,...,7 (eight numbers), and the trailing ':' begins the block of code that runs on each iteration.

Watch out for common errors: if you forget the ':' or the required indentation for the following line you get a syntax error; if you place the append line outside the loop by wrong indentation you will only collect one value instead of eight.
Be aware of a common misconception: range(8) does not include the number 8 — it runs eight times from 0 to 7. If you want a different count, change the number in range().

Best practices: if you do not use the loop variable, write 'for _ in range(8):' to show it is unused; consider using a clear prompt or validating input; alternatively, you can build the list with a comprehension if you prefer a shorter form once you understand it.

commentList: You append each user response to lst so the loop builds the list element by element; because this line is inside the for loop it runs eight times, producing eight list items.

You call input('Enter a value:') to show the prompt and receive a string; append(...) then adds that whole string as one list element. The input(...) call is evaluated first and its return value is passed as the single argument to lst.append.

Watch for common mistakes: if you write lst += input('...') you will add each character of the entered string as separate list items because a string is iterable. Also, forgetting to indent this line will cause an IndentationError. Note: in Python 3 input() returns a string (in Python 2 input() behaves differently, so use raw_input() there).

Best practices: make the prompt clearer by including the item number (for example f'Enter value {i+1}:'), consider stripping extra whitespace with .strip() like lst.append(input(...).strip()), and if you need numbers convert with int() inside a try/except to handle bad input.

commentList: You use print(lst) to show the final list on the screen so you can see the eight values you collected.
You are calling the print function with lst as its single argument; in Python 3 print needs parentheses and will convert the argument to a readable form before writing it to standard output.
You should expect to see Python's list representation: square brackets, commas, and each element shown as a string (with quotes) because input() returns strings.
You might get a NameError if lst was never created or was misspelled earlier, so make sure lst is defined before this line.
You might mistakenly expect numeric inputs to behave like numbers here — they are still strings unless you convert them before appending (for example with int() or float()).

For cleaner output you can use alternatives: print(*lst) to print values separated by spaces, ', '.join(lst) to print them as a comma-separated string (only for strings), or pprint.pprint(lst) for nicer formatting of complex lists.
Remember print adds a newline by default; if you need no newline or a different ending you can pass the end parameter (for example print(lst, end='')).

distractors.description: You might pick this because you think extend will add the user's entry to the list just like append. However, extend treats the input as an iterable and adds each character separately. For example, if you type hello, extend will add 'h','e','l','l','o' as five separate list elements, not the single string "hello". This breaks the program's intent to collect eight string values (you would end up with many more elements and fragmented strings). In addition, if the user enters an empty string nothing gets added. The key mistake is using an operation that expands the iterable instead of adding the entire input as a single list element.

You might select this because it looks like you're adding the input to the list, but you forgot the parentheses that call the input function. What this does is append the input function object itself to the list, not the text the user types. After running the loop you'd get the input function repeated eight times in the list (for example <built-in function input>), which is not the string values you wanted. There is no user prompt and no collected answers, so the program doesn't perform the intended input step. The mistake is treating the function name as if it were the function call that retrieves user data.

You might choose this because you think converting inputs to numbers is good practice. This line will convert the user's response to an integer before appending it. That leads to two issues: first, the program will store integers instead of strings, which contradicts the goal of creating a list of string values; second, if the user types any non-numeric text you'll get a runtime ValueError and the program will crash. The error risk and the change in data type make this line unsuitable when the task is to gather string inputs.
